correctness.rationale: For an origin-symmetric parallelotope P=A[-1,1]^3 with SVD A=QDR^T, the John principal-plane reflection pulls back to M=I-2vv^T with v a column of R. Origin symmetry removes translations from the relative circumradius, so its exact factor is ||M||_{infinity to infinity}. Orthogonality gives the universal sqrt(3) row-l1 bound. Equality forces one of two explicit squared-coordinate patterns. A direct radical comparison shows that an orthogonal equality pair must consist of opposite types with the same distinguished coordinate, and then its cross product has a zero coordinate, so an orthonormal equality triple is impossible. Thus some principal plane gives a strict factor below sqrt(3). The source's complementary-dimension and polarity identities transfer strictness to alpha_1 and to cross-polytopes; the Grundbacher-Kobos equality classification then excludes every remaining point-symmetric body.

evidence: Caragea et al. prove alpha_j(K) <= d_BM(K,B_2^n), complementary-dimension equality for point-symmetric bodies, and polarity invariance for origin-symmetric bodies, but leave the dimension-three attainment question open.
Grundbacher-Kobos prove that three-dimensional parallelotopes and cross-polytopes are exactly the symmetric bodies with Banach-Mazur distance sqrt(3) from the Euclidean ball.
Those broader results identify the only candidates but do not imply that their chirality is strictly smaller than sqrt(3).

value.rationale: The theorem gives a definitive negative answer to an explicit dimension-three attainment problem in the primary paper. It does so by a structural calculation on the exact candidate classes singled out by the literature, rather than by a numerical slice. The principal-axis infinity-norm formula and its equality-normal obstruction also identify why Banach-Mazur extremizers fail to be chirality extremizers, which is useful geometric information beyond the yes/no answer.
